If <note>grain and cloth</note> were used as currency, the damage and loss would be severe. They would be worn out and ruined in the hands of merchants, and wasted or discarded through being cut and divided for use. Viewed from this perspective, this proposal by Gong Yu <note>a Han dynasty minister who advocated abolishing metallic currency in favor of grain and silk</note> must certainly never be adopted. Even if in remote regions or subordinate districts people were tearing cloth or discarding grain to use them in place of coins, the authorities ought to prohibit such practices; how much less should this be established as statutory law?

During the reign of Emperor Huan of Han, a memorialist stated that because currency had become debased and goods devalued, the people were driven into poverty, and therefore the state ought to recast larger coins.

Liu Tao <note>a late Han dynasty official and scholar known for his frank counsel</note> said: "The present anxiety does not lie in currency, but in the famine of the people. For the people can go a century without currency, but cannot endure a single day of hunger; food is therefore the utmost urgency. Those debating this matter do not understand agriculture and cultivation."

<summary>Qiu Jun argues against substituting grain and textiles for metallic coin, noting the waste and damage caused by cutting cloth or handling grain. He then cites Han dynasty debates where Liu Tao maintained that addressing popular hunger took precedence over monetary reform.</summary>
<keywords>Qiu Jun, Gong Yu, Han dynasty, Emperor Huan, Liu Tao, currency, coinage, grain, cloth, famine, monetary policy</keywords>

Now, if one desires the people to be prosperous and wealth to multiply, the way lies in halting corvée labor and forbidding predatory exactions. Then the common people will have abundance without toil. Merely wanting to cast coins and equalize commodities to remedy these ills is like trying to nurture fish inside a boiling caldron, or roosting birds atop a raging fire. Water and trees are indeed what naturally give life to fish and birds, yet if used out of season, they inevitably lead to scorching and destruction.

Your minister observes: Liu Tao's statement that "the people can go a century without currency, but cannot endure a single day of hunger" is truly a profound truth. The reason the people suffer hunger is that they lack grain. Your minister wishes that our dynasty, when fixing market prices, would constantly treat rice and grain as the standard. Let an order be issued to the officials: within the capital, require the wards and markets to report the price of rice to the imperial court month by month; outside the capital, let the neighborhoods report daily to the district, and the districts report monthly

<summary>Qiu Jun concludes Liu Tao's memorial criticizing reliance on coinage over agricultural production, warning that minting money without halting labor and extortion is like boiling fish. Qiu Jun then endorses Liu Tao's view that food comes before currency, advising that official market prices always take grain as the fundamental standard and be tracked regularly.</summary>
<keywords>Qiu Jun, Liu Tao, Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, coinage, monetary policy, grain standard, market prices, rice, corvée labor, famine</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>to the prefecture; let the prefectures report each quarter to the provincial administration commissions; and let the provincial administration commissions report to the Ministry of Revenue. In this way, those in authority will know the exact quantities of money and grain. They may use this data to verify whether the people's food supply is sufficient, and devise methods for flexible circulation and reallocation. They must ensure that currency never reaches excessive surplus and grain never falls into shortage. When prices remain consistently stable, the people will suffer no hardship from hunger. As for other commodities, goods that the people may do with or without need not be calculated. Not only this, but one may also rely on these figures to determine corvée assignments, regulate tax levies, and plan public works.

Sun Quan of Wu first cast coins valued at one thousand <note>original: "當千錢"</note>. Yet these were excessively overvalued and held merely nominal worth, causing distress among the populace.

Your minister observes: The practice in later generations of casting nominal large coins <note>coins with face value far exceeding their metal worth</note> originated here. Now, Heaven establishes the ruler for the sake of the living people;

<summary>Qiu Jun explains how regular grain reports enable the government to balance food and money, stabilizing prices and preventing famine. He also notes that large, debased coins began under Sun Quan of Wu, bringing distress to the common people.</summary>
<keywords>Qiu Jun, Sun Quan, monetary policy, grain prices, Ministry of Revenue, price stabilization, famine prevention, taxation, corvée labor, debased coinage</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>the ruler is entrusted with overseeing the realm's wealth, not with monopolizing it for himself. Markets were established at midday so the people could barter and exchange goods to balance what they had with what they lacked. Yet when people traded goods for other goods, the desired items were not always on hand. For this reason, coinage was instituted. Goods and currency must correspond precisely in value without severe disparities or imbalance; only then can coinage circulate over a long period without ill effects. 

Rulers and ministers of later times, driven merely by deficits in state revenue, devised schemes of deceitful extortion to trick the people of the world. They seized the wealth of all under heaven and monopolized its profits for themselves. How could this ever be the will of Heaven in establishing a ruler? It was only natural that such measures ultimately failed to endure.

<summary>Qiu Jun argues that coinage was created to facilitate fair trade rather than to enrich the crown, condemning later rulers who debased currency for selfish profit. He then cites Southern Qi official Kong Yi on the structural problems of unbalanced coinage.</summary>
<keywords>Qiu Jun, Kong Yi, Southern Qi, Emperor Gao, monetary policy, coinage, commercial exchange, state monopoly, currency debasement, ethics of governance</keywords>

The forms and principles of heaven, earth, and the myriad things never escape the numbers of the <term>Xiantian</term> <gloss>Prior Heaven / Primordial Order</gloss>. Recently, upon examining the Diagram of the Ten Figures <note>original: "十相圖" (Shixiang tu)</note>, I realized even more clearly that indeed nothing fails to correspond with them. Yet because previous commentators may not have fully exhausted their explanation, I have briefly distinguished one or two matters concerning this in the treatise on the Three Powers in the opening volume.

The saying "assigning numbers based on three for heaven and two for earth" refers to establishing the operational numbers of the *Changes* by relying upon the correct standard numbers of heaven and earth. Heaven obtains three and thereby commands the whole, and therefore the permutations of the sun number thirty. Earth obtains two and divides the functions, and therefore the permutations of the moon number twelve. Combining the permutations of <term>yin</term> <gloss>receptive principle</gloss> and <term>yang</term> <gloss>active principle</gloss> yields forty-two, which is the product of six and seven: this marks a node of a single permutation in the Way of Heaven. Doubling this yields eighty-four, for where there is heaven there must be earth. Multiplying this by three yields two hundred and fifty-two, which is the culmination of the six permutations. Therefore, in the form of the human body, the portion from the kidneys up to the crown of the head belongs to heaven. Each permutation takes eight inches and four tenths as its node, culminating at two feet and five inches <note>and two tenths</note>

<summary>Zhang Xingcheng correlates the cosmological numbers of Prior Heaven and the Changes with solar, lunar, and human bodily proportions. He explains how mathematical multiples derived from heaven and earth govern cosmic cycles and the anatomy of the upper body.</summary>
<keywords>Xiantian, I Ching, Three Powers, numerology, solar cycles, lunar cycles, human anatomy, cosmology</keywords>

The two equinoxes mark the season of generated life in a single year: from when grass and trees begin to sprout until the ground freezes is likewise two hundred and fifty-two days. Therefore, the operational number is three hundred and sixty. Using seven parts out of ten yields the operational function of the operational number, which is two hundred and fifty-two. 

The *Treatise on the Three Powers* <note>original: "三才論" (Sancai lun)</note> states: from the kidneys to the heart is eight inches and four tenths; from the heart to the first ring of the windpipe <note>original: "重樓" (chonglou, literally "multistoried tower", an anatomical term for the trachea)</note> is eight inches and four tenths; from the windpipe to the crown of the head is eight inches and four tenths. From the kidneys to the crown of the head is two feet, five inches <note>and two tenths</note>. 

According to the Five Phases, five times five is the number of pure <term>yang</term> <gloss>active cosmic force</gloss>. This recognizes the permutations of five times five, but does not yet recognize the nodes of six times seven. For a male, at sixteen years of age the <term>tiangui</term> <gloss>reproductive vital essence</gloss> arrives, which corresponds to five thousand seven hundred and sixty days. Five thousand seven hundred and sixty is five hundred and seventy-six multiplied by ten. For a female, at fourteen years of age the <term>tiangui</term> arrives, which corresponds to five thousand and forty days. Five thousand and forty is five hundred and four

<summary>Zhang Xingcheng calculates cosmic and biological cycles using numerological multiples, demonstrating how seasonal growth periods, internal bodily dimensions, and the timing of human puberty align with mathematical ratios of the Changes.</summary>
<keywords>I Ching, Zhang Xingcheng, numerology, Three Powers, seasonal cycles, internal anatomy, tiangui, human development</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>multiplied by ten. Five hundred and seventy-six is two hundred and eighty-eight doubled. Two hundred and eighty-eight is six times eight, which is forty-eight, multiplied again by six; it is the number of eight. It is the application within substance, the operational number of Earth. Heaven follows Earth; therefore, a male corresponds to it through two times eight <note>sixteen years of age</note>. 

Five hundred and four is two hundred and fifty-two doubled. Two hundred and fifty-two is six times seven, which is forty-two, multiplied again by six; it is the number of seven. It is the application within application, the operational number of Heaven. Earth follows Heaven; therefore, a female corresponds to it through two times seven <note>fourteen years of age</note>. 

Fifteen corresponds to five thousand four hundred days. Five thousand four hundred is five hundred and forty multiplied by ten. It lies between fourteen and sixteen. Therefore, for the base number of the sixteen positions of the Imperial Ultimate <note>original: "皇極" (Huangji)</note>, each transformation uses fifty-four. Summing them yields two hundred and seventy; doubling it yields five

<summary>Zhang Xingcheng derives gendered maturation ages and cosmic cycle numbers from cosmological arithmetic, linking male and female developmental milestones to Heaven, Earth, and the transformations of the Imperial Ultimate.</summary>
<keywords>Zhang Xingcheng, numerology, I Ching, Huangji, Heaven and Earth, male and female maturation, tiangui, sixteen positions</keywords>

The *Treatise on the Three Powers* <note>original: "三才論" (Sancai lun)</note> states: "One thousand days of nursing and carrying; four thousand days of taking from external things and calculating according to Heaven and Earth; five thousand days, and one's <term>qi</term> <gloss>vital energy</gloss> becomes sufficient." Therefore, for a man at sixteen, his true essence is full; for a woman at fourteen, her true yin disperses. This recognizes the overarching principle of the five thousand days, but does not yet know the advancing and retreating of yin and yang. 

In ordinary people, with a single exhalation the pulse travels three inches; with a single inhalation the pulse travels three inches. One exhalation and one inhalation together constitute one breath, and the pulse travels six inches, because Heaven's three and Earth's three make the operation of six. In one day and one night, there are thirteen thousand five hundred breaths, and the pulse travels eight hundred and ten <term>zhang</term> <gloss>a traditional unit of length, approximately ten Chinese feet</gloss>, which is the number of nine times nine, or eighty-one. Thirteen thousand five hundred breaths yield twenty-seven thousand inhalations and exhalations. Twenty-seven thousand is the application of the number of substance: two hundred and seventy expanded to reach tens of thousands. This is also like the transformations of Heaven and Earth, which are eighty-four, while the bodily hair and pores have

<summary>Zhang Xingcheng synthesizes physiological respiration, pulse circulation, and developmental milestones with cosmic numerology, calculating daily breaths and pulse lengths through the mathematical principles of Heaven and Earth.</summary>

Generally speaking, when there are many bandits among the people, it is mostly due to insufficiency. When the people suffer from poverty, it is mostly due to excessive exactions from above. Once corrupt officials appear, the common people are thrown into turmoil and cannot peacefully remain in their traditional occupations, so many are driven to distress. How could there not be bandits? If a ruler simply maintains a state of not desiring <note>referring to Confucius's saying: "If you, sir, were not covetous, though you should reward them to do it, they would not steal" (Analects 12.18)</note>, how much vital energy <note>original: "元氣" (yuanqi), the fundamental vitality and economic resilience of the realm</note> is preserved for the local region! How many households are protected! When the water is ample, the fish grow large; when officials are clean and incorruptible, the people find peace. The single method of eliminating desire is truly seen to be an effective prescription for halting theft. One must not dismiss it as impractical talk.

### Chapter on Desiring Goodness <note>Analects 12.19: Ji Kangzi asked Confucius about government, saying, "What do you say to killing the unprincipled for the good of the principled?"</note>

The scholar Cai Yifan said: "Kangzi took the heart of killing as his place of practice <note>original: "道塲" (daochang, Sanskrit: bodhimaṇḍa), a sacred precinct or arena for cultivating realization</note>, whereas the Master took the <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>awakened mind / mind of universal compassion</gloss> as his place of practice." Zongjian said: "These words hold profound flavor. In this chapter, the phrase 'you conduct government' must be examined with great weight. To desire

<summary>Zhou Zongjian expounds on Confucius's teaching that popular theft stems from the greed of rulers, arguing that restraint among officials secures peace and livelihood. He then begins analyzing Analects 12.19, contrasting Ji Kangzi's punitive impulse with the Master's compassionate approach to governance.</summary>
<keywords>Analects commentary, Zhou Zongjian, Ji Kangzi, theft and poverty, governance, incorruptibility, bodhicitta, compassion</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>goodness, the character <term>desire</term> <gloss>yu</gloss> is like hunger needing food or thirst needing drink, never set aside for an instant. It is spoken directly from the genuine, vital sprout of one's heart. 'If you desire goodness, the people will be good' <note>Analects 12.19</note>: this dynamic is extremely swift, and it is entirely delineated upon the two characters 'governing' <note>original: "為政" (wei zheng)</note>. The next three sentences <note>Confucius's comparison: 'The virtue of the gentleman is like wind, and the virtue of the common people is like grass. When the wind moves over the grass, it must bend'</note> precisely show that one who governs finds it easy to inspire others. The commentator Tihu says that the line 'the virtue of the gentleman' carries the primary weight, while the following two lines are linked in explanation, turning back to expound upon the gentleman's virtue.

### Chapter on Being Distinguished and Gaining Renown <note>Analects 12.20, where Zizhang asks what a scholar must be like to be called distinguished (da), and Confucius contrasts genuine distinction with mere renown (wen)</note>

The students asked: "What is the overarching meaning and purpose of this entire chapter?" Zongjian said: "In the Master's school, nowhere is the distinction between sincerity and falsehood examined more thoroughly than in this chapter. It must be spoken with bold clarity, distinguishing whether something is one or two, severing and resolving the opposition between genuine distinction and superficial renown so thoroughly that not a single extraneous, vague word can enter. The two lines beginning 'Now as for distinction...' and 'Now as for renown...' cry out to set the contrast into motion."

<summary>Zhou Zongjian continues analyzing Analects 12.19 on moral influence in governance, citing commentator Tihu on the metaphor of wind and grass. He then begins Analects 12.20, answering students on the rigorous moral distinction between genuine spiritual distinction and mere superficial renown.</summary>
<keywords>Analects 12.19, Analects 12.20, Zhou Zongjian, Tihu, virtue of the gentleman, wind and grass, distinction versus renown, da and wen, sincerity and falsehood</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>must be examined with such vivid, waking alertness. When looking at the entire section on <term>distinction</term> <gloss>da</gloss>, one must closely align it with the underlying purpose and thrust of this chapter.

The phrase 'straightforward in quality and loving righteousness' <note>Analects 12.20</note> expresses his unadorned simplicity and lack of showiness. The two phrases 'examining words and observing expressions' express his restraint and lack of wantonness. The commentary's gloss 'what he does is appropriate' differs from what is elsewhere called 'making adaptations according to the times'. A scholar of genuine hidden cultivation merely does what should be done according to his proper station. He never engages in bizarre, extraordinary behavior, abandoning his basic duty to perform shocking, world-startling acts. This is precisely the starting point of his hidden cultivation.

'Examining and observing' does not mean spying on the pleasure or anger of others. It entirely speaks to his own self-reckoning, self-questioning, carefulness, and reverent vigilance. The Sage deliberately set down this phrase as a foundation for 'bearing oneself with humility before others' <note>original: "慮以下人" (lu yi xia ren)</note>, and it carries absolutely no sense of scrutinizing oneself in calculation. 'Bearing oneself with humility' means holding oneself back in restraint and self-effacement, refusing to assume an elevated, grandiose, or sprawling appearance, and being without

<summary>Zhou Zongjian explains Confucius's definition of true distinction in Analects 12.20, analyzing inner qualities such as unadorned uprightness, propriety in one's station, and watchful restraint. He clarifies that examining words and demeanor is self-reflective vigilance rather than calculating others' moods, serving as the basis for genuine humility.</summary>
<keywords>Analects 12.20, Zhou Zongjian, genuine distinction, hidden cultivation, straightforward in quality, loving righteousness, examining words and expressions, humility before others, self-restraint</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: and being without</meta> apprehension or fear of consequences, not being the opposite of arrogant pride. If one interprets this as mere modest compliance, one completely misses the original core meaning.

As for the section on <term>notoriety</term> <gloss>wen</gloss>, every single sentence stands in direct contrast to what came before. These are all schemes within the trap of fame. They represent those scholars of a degenerate age who engage in empty talk about heart-mind and moral nature. The essential tone and meaning of the phrase 'straightforward in quality' means that throughout his life, he is simple and honest, not engaging in cosmetic embellishment. When it comes to his actions, he single-mindedly seeks only what is fitting and proper. To be straightforward in quality is intrinsically the basic capacity of loving righteousness; it is not that outside of this straightforward quality one supplements it with worldly tact. Treat 'quality' as the opposite of cosmetic embellishment. Treat 'straightforward' as the opposite of feigned deceit. A sincere heart has only one straight path, with no winding deviations. But a false heart has thousands of twisting byways and paths.

Zou Zhaomin <note>Zou Yuanbiao, 1551–1624, prominent Ming dynasty scholar and Donglin leader</note> said: The phrase 'Now, one who possesses distinction' extends straight through to both occurrences of 'will certainly attain distinction'. The phrase 'Now, one who possesses notoriety' extends straight through to both occurrences of 'will certainly attain notoriety'. Only because he is certain to attain distinction is he called distinguished; only because he is certain to attain notoriety is he called notorious. This statement

<summary>Zhou Zongjian continues analyzing Analects 12.20, arguing that genuine straightforwardness is sincere righteousness without cosmetic pretension or artificial tact, contrasted with empty seekers of fame. He cites Ming scholar Zou Yuanbiao to emphasize the structural and moral distinction between true inner attainment and outward reputation.</summary>
<keywords>Analects 12.20, Zhou Zongjian, Zou Zhaomin, Zou Yuanbiao, distinction versus notoriety, straightforwardness, sincerity, empty talk, moral nature</keywords>

Banner-Embroidered Flag
The Book of Han <note>original: "Han Shu"</note>, in the Biography of Chen Tang, states: Chen Tang looked from afar and saw five-colored <term>banner-flags</term> <gloss>fan zhi</gloss> erected upon the Chanyu's city walls. Crown Ribbons
The Book of Wei <note>original: "Wei Shu"</note>, in the Annals of Emperor Shizong, records an imperial edict from the third year of the Jingming era <note>502 AD</note> stating: "Agriculture and sericulture are the foundation of the people, while the state reveres the rites of sericulture and the sacred plowing field. Upon these depend the sacrificial grain offerings, and on these relies the crown's silken ribbons."

Thin Fabric
The Discourses on Salt and Iron <note>original: "Yantie Lun"</note> states: Fine gauzes, silk crepes, patterned brocades, and embroideries are the garments of rulers, princes, and royal consorts; cocoon silks, wild pongee, thick silk, and white refined silk are the auspicious adornments of marriages. For this reason, patterned damasks and thin fabrics are not sold commonly in the ordinary market.

A Single Weave
Dai Fugu, in his "Song of White Ramie Fabric" <note>original: "Bai Zhu Ge"</note>, wrote: "With snow as the weft and jade as the warp, woven by hand into three lengths in a single weave."

Rhyme Lexicon Additions:
Provisioning and Feeding
The Ode to the Hundred-Li District <note>original: "Bai Li Fu"</note> states: "Delivering the wrapped sheaves." The commentary explains: "Grain straw is called zong <note>original: "總"</note>. It was brought in to feed the state's horses."

Raising and Feeding
The Book of Northern Qi <note>original: "Bei Qi Shu"</note>, in the Biography of Bai Jian, states: In the third year of the Heqing era <note>564 AD</note>, when the Turks invaded the territory, the herds of fine horses from the Dai and Xin pastures, totaling tens of thousands of head, were sheltered in the cypress valleys north of Mount Wutai to avoid the marauders. After the raiders retreated, an imperial decree ordered Bai Jian to inspect the herds. Later, envoys were sent to Bai Jian to take custody of the horses and deliver them to Dingzhou, entrusting them to the local population to raise and feed.

Awaiting Feed
The Book of Tang <note>original: "Tang Shu"</note>, in the Biography of Lu Zhi, states: Lu Zhi noted that soldiers were levied every year from Henan, the Huai River, and the Yangtze River regions to defend the northwest borders against autumn incursions, an operation called "Autumn Defense." The soldiers were not properly trained and repeatedly suffered defeats. Because the commanders did not have unified control, they could not counter the enemy effectively. Lu Zhi therefore submitted a memorial outlining these defects, stating: "Counting the days until their return, they merely open their mouths awaiting food. If the army suffers even a single setback, they exploit the danger and confusion, scattering eastward across the roads. In peacetime, state funds and reserves are exhausted to support idle surplus troops; when crisis strikes, cities and garrisons are abandoned, shaking the borderlands."

### Forage and Fodder <note>original: "秣飼"</note>

Essential Techniques for the Peasantry <note>original: "Qi Min Yao Shu"</note> states: In training and preparing implements and gear, strive to make them swift and sharp; in providing forage and fodder <note>original: "秣飼"</note> to cattle and livestock, always keep them fat and sturdy.

The Prime Tortoise of the Record Bureau <note>original: "Cefu Yuangui"</note> records that in the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era <note>792 AD</note>, Pei Yanling submitted a memorial stating: "Stable horses in the winter months ought to be kept at the manger and provided forage and fodder <note>original: "秣飼"</note>; in midsummer, there must be pastures for grazing. Your servant has recently investigated and found that on the borders of Chang'an and Xianyang counties, there are several hundred qing of ponds and wetlands; I request that these be designated as grazing grounds for the internal stables."

Cao Tang, in his poem A Sick Horse, writes: "One morning, the aspiration to cover a thousand miles still remains; how could it be willing secretly to forget the kindness of forage and fodder <note>original: "秣飼"</note>?"

Shi Jie, in a poem, writes: "With fine grain and lush grass, the official of the ten stables provides forage and fodder <note>original: "秣飼"</note>."

### Watering and Feeding <note>original: "飲飼"</note>

Essential Techniques for the Peasantry <note>original: "Qi Min Yao Shu"</note> states: When employing oxen and riding horses, gauge their strength and capacity. If warmth and cold, watering and feeding <note>original: "飲飼"</note> suit their natural dispositions, there has never been a case where they did not become fat, robust, and prolific.

### Summoning to Feast <note>original: "召飼"</note>

Further Discussions from the Eastern Library <note>original: "Dongguan Yulun"</note> notes: Liu Yuanfu transcribed the inscription of the Ju Zhong Yi in clerical script, which reads: "Ju Zhong made this precious grain vessel; selecting fine metal, both sharp and molten, along with furnaces; its silk red, its black, its yellow, to hold various flags and offerings of grain and rice, used to make grand, correct music; the king bestowed banquets and provisions, gathering them to summon and feast <note>original: "召飼"</note>. May Ju Zhong receive boundless fortune, certainly sharing in meals and provisions at the lodging, granting Ju Zhong long life."

### Nourished Without Food <note>original: "如飼"</note>

Biographies of the Immortals <note>original: "Shenxian Zhuan"</note> records: Shen Jian once set out on a distant journey and entrusted a bondmaid, three male servants, a donkey, and ten sheep to a host, giving each a single medicinal pill. He said to the host: "I only burden your house; do not trouble yourself with drink or food for them." After Jian departed, the host offered drink and food to the servants, but upon smelling the aroma of food, they all retched and vomited, declining to consume anything. When grass was fed to the donkey and sheep, the donkey and sheep turned away and would not eat. After more than one hundred days, the appearance of the servants was sleek and radiant, far surpassing how they looked when eating ordinary food; the donkey and sheep were all plump.

### Provisioning with Grain <note>original: "餉飼"</note>

Records of the Assembled Immortals of the Walled City <note>original: "Yongcheng Jixian Lu"</note> records: An old man said to Bian Dongxuan: "From your youth until now, forty years have passed. For thirty years, you have stored up the five grains to provision and feed <note>original: "餉飼"</note> birds and insects; calculated this way, the cost is no less than the price of elixirs."

One passage states: "Like alarm and commiseration at the initial instant of an infant falling into a well, at the time when one is just about to feel alarm and commiseration, but has not yet formed alarm and commiseration." Examining what Luzhai stated, it was fundamentally based on this passage. When reflecting upon it deeply, an obstacle ultimately remains: once one has said that alarm and commiseration arise at the initial instant an infant falls into a well, how can one also speak of not yet forming alarm and commiseration?

Another passage states: "When a person today suddenly sees an infant about to fall into a well, because movement is triggered, the heart of commiseration is seen. When there is not yet an infant about to fall into a well, this mind has not moved, and is simply stillness." This distinction is drawn cleanly and clearly. From this, one knows that in the former passage the recorder must not have fully understood, or there were erroneous characters. Luzhai happened to see the former passage and did not consult the latter passage, hence this oversight occurred. The *Recorded Sayings* were completed by the hands of many disciples. Where there are doubtful points, one ought to cross-examine and harmonize the multitude of statements in seeking the truth. One must not hastily grasp a single saying and take it as the final conclusion.

# At the mourning of an officer, when the grand encoffining is about to take place, the ruler is not present. The remainder of the ritual accords with that of a grand master.

<note>Correct Meaning</note> Zheng Kangcheng states: "The remainder" refers to the positions of the ministers, grand masters, and the mistress of the house, the spreading of the shrouding garments, and the proper ceremonial positions and decorum for men and women, all of which accord with the rites for a grand master.

Kong Yingda's sub-commentary states: This clarifies the proper ritual stages of an officer's encoffining. An officer's mourning rank is humble and involves no special imperial favor, so the ruler does not personally oversee the encoffining. Hence the text says, "the ruler is not present." If a grand master is present and the ruler happens to attend, the positions of the ministers and grand masters would also be located at the edge of the hall near the western steps.

Top Six: Wading across the stream until the water submerges the crown of the head. Misfortune, but no blame. The Commentary on the Image says: The misfortune of wading across cannot be blamed.

<term>Yichuan</term> <gloss>Cheng Yi, Song dynasty Neo-Confucian philosopher</gloss> stated: The Top Six, by means of yin yielding, dwells at the extreme of exceeding. This represents the petty person who carries the transgression of the ordinary to the utmost extreme. What is termed "great exceeding" in the case of a petty person does not mean being able to accomplish deeds that greatly surpass ordinary men. It merely means transgressing the normal and violating principle, showing no regard for peril or ruin, and stepping directly into danger and disaster. It is like wading across deep water to the point that it submerges the top of one's head: its misfortune is obvious. The petty person acts with rash frenzy and thereby brings calamity upon himself; this is indeed what he deserves. Whom else then can one blame?

# <term>Kan</term> <gloss>The Abysmal Water hexagram</gloss>

<term>Yichuan</term> <gloss>Cheng Yi, Song dynasty Neo-Confucian philosopher</gloss> stated: <term>Xi</term> <gloss>repeated / practiced</gloss> means repeated practice. Although other hexagrams are doubled, the word is not added to their names. <term>Kan</term> alone adds <term>Xi</term> <note>forming Xi Kan, Repeated Pit / Repeated Water</note> because it signifies repeated danger. Within danger there is again danger; its significance is profound. 

In general, when a yang line is at the top, it is the image of stopping <note>Gen, Mountain</note>. When in the middle, it is the image of entrapment and falling into danger <note>Kan, Water</note>. When at the bottom, it is the image of movement <note>Zhen, Thunder</note>. When a yin line is at the top, it is the image of joy and speaking <note>Dui, Lake</note>. When in the middle, it is the image of clinging and brilliance <note>Li, Fire</note>. When at the bottom, it is the image of following and entering <note>Xun, Wind</note>. Entrapment constitutes danger. <term>Xi</term> means repetition, as in learning and reviewing; both carry the meaning of repetition. <term>Kan</term> is danger; what the hexagram discusses is the proper way to conduct oneself in danger and adversity. <term>Kan</term> is water; the number One begins in the middle, being the earliest of generated things; therefore it represents water. Plunging downward is the essential nature of water.

<term>Nanxuan</term> <gloss>Zhang Shi, Song dynasty Neo-Confucian scholar</gloss> stated: <term>Qian</term> <gloss>Heaven</gloss> leads the chant while <term>Kun</term> <gloss>Earth</gloss> harmonizes. <term>Qian</term> is exalted while <term>Kun</term> is humble. This arises from nature and cannot be altered.

Water has a constant flow and depends on nothing, whereas fire must attach itself to firewood before its form can become visible. <term>Gen</term> is mountain, and <term>Dui</term> is lake. The mountain can thickly sustain all things and give them life and growth, whereas the lake, if not acting through other things, cannot bestow its moistening nourishment. Gather herbs and medicines in a dispensary, providing them with suitable lodgings. Shamans must reside near the public altar <note>original: "公社" (gongshe), the communal altar of the soil and state</note> and show reverent devotion to the spirits. The shamans and diviners shall petition the defender <note>the military commander in charge of city defense</note>, but the defender alone holds ultimate authority. When shamans and diviners observe atmospheric omens <note>original: "望氣" (wangqi), the ancient practice of reading vapor, clouds, and qi to predict military fortunes</note>, they report their findings and do nothing more. If they spread rumors entering or leaving the grounds, terrifying and alarming officials and common people, investigate their actions with strict precision and sentence them without pardon.

The quarters for those who read atmospheric omens must be placed close to the defender. As for government herdsmen, worthy ministers, and those possessing specialized technical crafts <note>original: "方技" (fangji)</note>, house and provision them according to their ranking, just as with skilled artisans. Gather butchers and cooks, placing them in the kitchens to supply necessities, each graded by rank.

As a general rule for city defense, the district commander <note>original: "縣師" (xianshi), a military administrative officer</note> receives his commission, brings forth stored provisions, patrols the ditches and embankments, builds palisades, clears thoroughfares, and repairs the city walls. The various officials contribute resources, and the diverse artisans apply themselves to their tasks. The master of the horse <note>original: "司馬" (sima), the chief military official</note> inspects the wall repairs, organizes the ranks of soldiers, and arranges the gate guards. Three men manage the right gate, two men manage the left gate, and four men manage closing the gates. A hundred armored soldiers sit inside. On top of the city walls, opposite the access stairs, assigned officers shall stand guard. Urgent reports from inside or outside shall be gathered in the field and transmitted promptly. Every soldier shall have an assigned post.

Beyond the city walls, within the reach of falling arrows, demolish the buildings and walls so that approaching enemies cannot find shelter or construct siege platforms <note>original: "菌" (jun), referring here to enemy siege towers or assault shelters</note>. Within thirty leagues <note>original: "里" (li)</note>, gather all firewood, fodder, and stored water into the city. Collect all dogs, pigs, piglets, and fowl to eat their flesh, and gather their bones to brew broth and meat paste to nourish and restore those sickened with abdominal illnesses.

Inside the city, plaster all firewood, fodder, and dwellings within arrow reach with mud to prevent fires. Issue orders that at dusk dogs must be muzzled, horses gagged, and ropes tied <note>to keep quiet and prevent noise</note>. In the quiet of the night, upon hearing the sound of drums, respond with counterfeit calls, for this is how one breaks the enemy's morale and steadies the resolve of the people. Therefore, when deceptive signals are sounded at the proper moments, the people will not succumb to panic or sickness.

The ritual scribes and diviners shall then announce prayers at the distant altars, to the four sacred peaks, the rivers, and the altars of the soil and grain. Perform these rites before the military departs, and then withdraw. The ruler, clad in plain unadorned robes of mourning, shall make solemn vows at the Grand Ancestral Temple.

After the solemn oath was administered, the Duke retired to take his meal and lodged in a chamber to the right of the Grand Ancestral Temple. The ritual scribes and diviners lodged at the altar of the soil. All officials were fully prepared for duty. Thereupon, war drums were sounded. To the right of the gate a falcon banner <note>original: "旂" (qi), a flag depicting raptors or falcons</note> was erected, and to the left of the gate a feather pennant <note>original: "旌" (jing), an ox-tail or feather staff standard</note> was planted. At the corner tower, chosen archers were assembled and shot three volleys to announce impending victory. The five types of weapons were all readied. Then the troops descended the walls, marched forth, and mounted watchtowers to gaze toward our outer suburbs. Orders were then given to sound the drums.

Presently, the garrison forces climbed the ramparts. The marshal of troops shot from the right of the gate; upon meeting the enemy's arrows, he shot back, discharging three arrow volleys <note>original: "茅" (mao), used here in military contexts for arrow projectiles or signals</note>, followed in succession by the archers and crossbowmen. The garrison commander shot from the left of the gate, first casting throwing beams, followed by boulders. The ritual scribes and clansmen then announced prayers to the altar of the soil, covering the sacred vessel with an earthen steamer <note>original: "甑" (zeng), a clay pot or steamer used in solemn protective ritual concealment</note>.

If clarity relies solely on one's own initiative, one's virtue will not be broad. Therefore, even though a woman represents yielding and darkness, one should still accept whatever good she offers; then one's clarity will be expansive. Moreover, because the other lines are all yin <gloss>yielding</gloss>, it is said that the second line can embrace and accept. Thus, it can assist in the affairs of its ruler, just as a son can manage his household. That a son is able to govern the household is due to the father's undivided trust. The second line and the fifth line connect through the mutual feeling of firmness and yielding; hence, the second line is able to enact the way of firmness and central balance, achieving the merit of enlightening youthful ignorance <note>original: "發蒙", referring to Hexagram 4, Meng</note>.

In terms of status and hierarchy, the fifth line represents the way of the father, while the second line represents the way of the son. In terms of hexagram qualities, the second line serves as the teacher to the fifth. The Sage feared that the nine in the second place <note>the firm second line</note> might presume upon the role of teacher and thereby lose the proper duty of a minister and son. Therefore, the Sage admonished him with the words "the son managing the household" <note>original: "子克家"</note>.

<term>Yichuan</term> <gloss>Cheng Yi, Song dynasty philosopher</gloss> stated: The third line, being yin and yielding <note>original: "以隂柔"</note>, dwells in youthful ignorance and darkness. It is neither central nor correct, representing a woman who acts rashly and recklessly. Her proper corresponding partner is in the upper position <note>the top line</note>, yet she cannot bring herself to follow someone far away. Seeing nearby that the nine in the second place is where the multitude of the ignorant converge, enjoying the height of timely success, she abandons her proper correspondence and attaches herself to him. This is what is meant by a woman seeing a "man of bronze" <note>original: "金夫", literally a wealthy or metallic husband, symbolizing material wealth and immediate power</note>. When a woman joins herself to another, she should follow proper ritual propriety. Yet here, seeing another's great wealth, she is delighted and follows him, unable to protect or preserve her own person. There is nowhere she may go that is advantageous. When a woman behaves in this manner, her conduct is perverse, depraved, and contrary to propriety; she must not be taken in marriage.

<term>Chengzhai</term> <gloss>Yang Wanli, Song dynasty scholar</gloss> said: To be obstructed from passage is called distress; to be stingy in following others is called stinginess. Those stingy regarding illness hide their condition from physicians; those stingy regarding their faults hide their errors from teachers. The fourth line is beset by ignorance, and furthermore is stingy in drawing close to worthy men; is this not what Confucius called being beset by ignorance yet refusing to learn, which makes the common people the lowest class?

Yang is bright, while Yin is dark; Yang is solid, while Yin is hollow. Nine in the second place serves as the master of the entire hexagram for dispelling ignorance. All four Yin lines rely on it to dispel their ignorance: the initial line and the third line are in close contact with it; the six in the fifth place corresponds with it; only the fourth line remains distant from it. Its distress and stinginess are thus entirely brought upon itself.

# Volume 29

My late grandfather held the titles of Grand Master <note>original: "大夫", a high civil rank</note>, Manager of Affairs for the Jiangnan Branch Secretariat <note>original: "江南行中書省平章政事"</note>, Upper Pillar of State <note>original: "上柱國", an honorary civil title</note>, Minister of Works <note>original: "司徒", literally Grand Minister of Education/Works</note>, and Duke of Wu; my late grandmother Wang was the Duchess of Wu. My late father held the prestigious rank of Palace Emissary with the Threefold Dignities <note>original: "開府儀同三司", granting ceremonial parity with the Three Excellencies</note>, Administrator of Military and State Affairs, Right Chancellor of the Campaign to Pacify the West, and Duke of Wu; my late mother Chen was the Duchess of Wu. On the thirteenth day of the intercalary month, we respectfully paid reverence at the ancestral tombs, burning incense and making sacrificial announcements in accordance with ancestral rites.

Reflecting deeply upon the duty to repay one's roots, the rituals performed must be bountiful. The achievements and deeds we strive to establish today do not stem from our own abilities, but rather rely on the enduring spiritual protection and abundant blessings bestowed by prior generations, extending their favor to future descendants. To repay the grace of three generations and have them all enfeoffed as Dukes fulfills the utmost heartfelt wish of their descendants. The *Classic of Documents* states: "Upon those who do good, Heaven sends down all blessings." The *Book of Changes* states: "A family that accumulates good deeds will surely have surplus prosperity." Our late grandfather accumulated virtuous deeds and merits; the recompense from Heaven is rich and flourishing.

In the generations that follow, all my descendants should embody the heart of our ancestors, tread in virtue, and preserve benevolence, so that their lineage may be perpetuated boundlessly without end. This is my deepest hope. Thereupon, I set down this record in full at the end, so that it may be transmitted as true witness and serve as a reference for future generations.

<note>Author's appraisal:</note> The Ming lineage originally traced its descent from the mythical emperor <term>Zhuanxu</term> <gloss>a legendary sovereign of ancient China</gloss>. In the Zhou dynasty, feudal lords had their state at Zhu; they were also the descendants of Zhu Fu, the Minister of Works <note>original: "司空"</note> under the Han dynasty. Yet Ming Emperor Taizu <note>original: "太祖", posthumous temple name of the Hongwu Emperor, Zhu Yuanzhang</note> refused to falsely attach himself to famous and distinguished clans. Instead, he took only his earliest known ancestor, <term>Dezu</term> <gloss>posthumous title bestowed on Emperor Taizu's great-great-grandfather, Zhu Baoliu</gloss>, as the founding forefather. His breadth of insight and integrity in this regard far surpassed the rulers of the Han and Tang dynasties.

The Earl of Zheng brought to justice those who had participated in the rebellion of Yong Jiu <note>a former plot to assassinate the minister Zhai Zhong on behalf of Duke Li</note>. ## Ling Hill <note>original: Ling Qiu</note>

**Mencius**: Mencius said to Chiwa, "Your resignation of the post of governor of **Ling Hill** <note>original: Ling Qiu</note> to request an appointment as master of justice seemed appropriate, because as master of justice you had the opportunity to speak out."

**Records of the Grand Historian**: In the Basic Annals of the House of Zhao, in the second year of Marquis Jing, he defeated the state of Qi at **Ling Hill**.
**Classic of Waterways**: The Kou River emerges from Gao Mountain in **Ling Hill** County of Dai Commandery.
Also, **Inner Biography of Emperor Wu of Han**: Among secondary medicines are the liver of the white phoenix from Meng Mountain and the blood of the green mythical bird from **Ling Hill**.
**Ji Kang’s Poem**: Riding the high wind on a distant journey, climbing high upon **Ling Hill**.
**Liu Shao’s Rhapsody on the Capital of Zhao**: To its west lies the level orchard of **Ling Hill**, sloping upward to meet the Kunlun mountains.

## Qin Hill <note>original: Qin Qiu</note>

**Records of the Grand Historian**: In the Biographies of Humorous Figures, King Zhuang of Chu summoned the son of Sunshu Ao and enfeoffed him with four hundred households at **Qin Hill**, so that he might maintain ancestral offerings to his father.
**Book of the Later Han**: In the Treatise on Commanderies and Kingdoms, the district of Gushi contains **Qin Hill**.

## Fuqiu <note>original: Fuqiu</note>

**Book of Han**: In the Biography of King Yuan of Chu, when King Yuan, Liu Jiao, was young, he studied the Book of Songs under Master Fuqiu together with Mu Sheng, Bai Sheng, and Master Shen of Lu.
Also, **Book of Tang**: In the Treatise on Literature, there is the *Classic of Assessing Cranes* in one scroll by Master **Fuqiu**.
**Biographies of Immortals**: Wangzi Qiao was Prince Jin, son of King Ling of Zhou. He was fond of playing the reed pipes to imitate the song of the phoenix, roaming between the Yi and Luo rivers. The Daoist immortal Master **Fuqiu** received him and led him up Mount Song. After more than thirty years, when people sought him upon the mountain, he appeared to Huan Liang and said, "Tell my family to wait for me on the seventh day of the seventh month at the summit of Mount Goushi." When the appointed time arrived, he indeed came riding a white crane, pausing atop the mountain. He raised his hands to bid farewell to the people of the world, departing several days later.
**Guo Pu’s Poem**: With my left hand I gather the sleeves of **Fuqiu**; with my right hand I pat the shoulder of Hongya.
**Liu Xiaowei’s Poem**: Who can match the phoenix melody? Only Master **Fuqiu**.

## Jie Hill <note>original: Jie Qiu, Grand Hill</note>

**Book of Han**: In the Biography of Sima Xiangru, it states that when the Zhou dynasty experienced the auspicious omen of the leaping fish and the shooting star, they commemorated them with sacrificial fires, though these were minor signs. If one were to use such portents to ascend **Jie Hill** <note>original: Jie Qiu</note> to perform the Feng and Shan sacrifices, would one not feel ashamed? Fu Qian’s commentary notes that *jie* means great and *qiu* means hill; it indicates that for the Zhou house to take a white fish as an auspicious omen and ascend Mount Tai to perform the sacrifices would surely evoke shame.
**Book of Jin**: In the Treatise on Ritual, it states that among the rulers of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties who brought order to their age and performed great achievements, none failed to respectfully receive Heaven's grace, harmoniously comply with the aspirations of the people, ascend **Jie Hill** <note>original: Jie Qiu</note>, and tread upon Mount Liangfu. None of them ever declined this, for it was truly something that could not be yielded.
**Liu Bin’s Poem**: I wait to hear of the seasoned cauldron's savory broth; soon you shall attend the sacrifices at **Jie Hill** <note>original: Jie Qiu</note>.
**Lu Zhaolin’s Poem**: Emerald phoenixes wind their way ascending **Jie Hill** <note>original: Jie Qiu</note>; immortal cranes linger wandering high in the heavens.

## One Hill <note>original: Yi Qiu</note>

**Book of Han**: In the Biography of Yang Yun, it states that the ancients and moderns are like jackals of the **same hill** <note>original: yi qiu zhi he, proverbial for beings of the same cut or ilk</note>.
Also, in the Autobiographical Preface: Fishing by a single gorge, myriad things cannot alter his purpose; dwelling at ease on **one hill** <note>original: yi qiu</note>, all under heaven cannot exchange his joy.
**Book of Jin**: In the Eulogy of the Biography of Xie An, the Grand Protection's rise and fall was vast as an empty boat, his station elevated above all dukes and ministers, yet his heart's desire remained solely with **one hill** <note>original: yi qiu, signifying a secluded recluse retreat</note>.
Also, in the Biography of Xie Kun, Emperor Ming asked him: "Those who discuss character compare you with Yu Liang. How do you regard yourself?" He replied: "Standing solemnly in court robes within the ancestral temple to serve as a standard for all officials, Kun is not the equal of Liang. But facing **one hill** <note>original: yi qiu</note> and one ravine, I consider myself superior."
**Song Jing’s Poem**: Looking northward, I merely revere the twin palace gates; gazing southward, I enjoy the beauty of **one hill** <note>original: yi qiu</note>.
**Wu Pingyi’s Poem**: Ringing carriage bells glisten brightly descending multi-storied pavilions; feathered canopies wander leisurely toward **one hill** <note>original: yi qiu</note>.
**Su Shi’s Poem**: Sun and moon turn like twin wheels; ancient and modern share the **same hill** <note>original: yi qiu</note>.
Also, in the **History of the Southern Dynasties**: In the Biography of Qiu Zhongfu, when he was promoted to Magistrate of Shanyin, his governance was held in very high repute. The common folk sang a ballad saying: "The two Chuans, Shen, and Liu, are not the equal of **one Qiu** <note>original: yi qiu, a pun on the surname Qiu and one hill</note>." Formerly, Chuan Yan and his son, Shen Xian, and Liu Xuanming had successively governed Shanyin, all leaving records of excellent administration; this ballad declared that Zhongfu surpassed them all.

All images and underlying principles of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things never escape the numbers of the Prior Heaven <term>xiantian</term> <gloss>a cosmological model representing the primordial order of the universe before physical manifestation</gloss>. Recently, upon examining the Diagram of the Ten Aspects, I recognized even more clearly that indeed nothing fails to conform to it. Yet what previous commentators have expressed was perhaps not exhaustive, so in the opening volume's discourse on the Three Powers <term>sancai</term> <gloss>the cosmic triad of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity</gloss>, I briefly discriminated one or two matters.

Regarding the principle that "Heaven takes three and Earth takes two, and upon these the numbers are based" <note>original: "三天兩地而倚數"</note>, it means establishing numbers by relying on the proper, fundamental numbers of Heaven and Earth. This constitutes the functioning numbers of the Book of Changes <term>Yijing</term> <gloss>the ancient Chinese divination manual and cosmological text</gloss>. Heaven obtains three and thus unifies the whole; therefore the transformations of the sun number thirty. Earth obtains two and thus distributes its functions; therefore the transformations of the moon number twelve. Combining the transformations of yin and yang yields forty-two, which is the product of six and seven, marking the nodal measure of a single transformation in the Course of Heaven. Doubling it yields eighty-four, for where there is Heaven there must also be Earth. Tripling this again yields two hundred fifty-two, which is the culmination of six transformations. 

Therefore, in the human form, the region from the kidneys to the crown of the head belongs to the division of Heaven. Each transformation takes eight inches and four tenths as its nodal measure, culminating at two feet five inches and two tenths.

<summary>Zhang Xingcheng explains the cosmological mathematics of the Yijing, showing how the numbers assigned to Heaven (three) and Earth (two) govern solar and lunar cycles as well as the proportions of the human body.</summary>

The line 'upright in nature and loving righteousness' speaks of being simple, genuine, and unpretentious. The two lines 'examining people's words and observing their demeanor' speak of being restrained and not unrestrained. 'Acting appropriately' in the commentary differs from 'adapting actions according to the times' elsewhere. A scholar truly engaged in hidden cultivation simply does what ought to be done within his proper station in life, never acting bizarrely or strangely, nor abandoning his duty to perform some extraordinary deed that shocks the world and frightens common folk. This is precisely where his hidden cultivation takes hold.

'Examining' and 'observing' do not mean prying into other people's pleasure or anger; they speak entirely of examining oneself, doubting oneself, and maintaining vigilance and caution. The sage specifically set down these words to lay the foundation for humility toward others, completely devoid of any intention to examine oneself excessively. Being humble toward others means restraining and holding oneself back, not adopting a lofty, grand, and expansive demeanor, and not

The section on <term>wen</term> <gloss>reputation</gloss> stands in complete opposition to the section above; both are schemes born within the snare of fame. This refers precisely to those scholars of later times who speak emptily of mind and human nature. The phrase 'upright in nature' generally means that throughout one's life one remains straightforward and honest, refusing to indulge in superficial embellishment, and in all one's conduct one seeks only to accord with what is fitting. Being upright in nature is fundamentally the foundation for loving righteousness; it is not that one balances uprightness by adding worldly smoothness. 'Uprightness of nature' should be viewed against superficial embellishment; 'straightforwardness' should be viewed against pretense and falsehood. A sincere heart follows only a single road, with no crooked bends; but a deceitful heart gives rise to a thousand paths and ten thousand trails.

## Pronunciation: Yang-Li Phonetic Reading, to Feed <note>original: "洋吏切食", rhyme heading for 飼 (si)</note>
Pronunciation note: Xiang-Li phonetic reading, to feed.
Meaning: To feed, to nourish; identical with the character 飤.

### Rhyme Vocabulary Additions: Supply Feed <note>original: "增供飼"</note>
The Rhapsody on Hundred-Mile Regions from the Classic of History <note>original: "Shu Bai Li Fu"</note> states: Presenting grain bundles, where the commentary notes that zong refers to stalks of grain. It was contributed to supply feed for the state's horses.

### Raise and Feed <note>original: "養飼"</note>
The Book of Northern Qi <note>original: "Bei Qi Shu"</note>, in the Biography of Bai Jian, records: In the third year of the Heqing era <note>564 AD</note>, the Tujue Turks invaded the borders. The two imperial horse pastures of Dai and Xin held tens of thousands of fine steeds. They were all hidden in the cypress valleys north of Mount Wutai to evade the enemy bandits. After the bandits retreated, an imperial edict ordered Bai Jian to inspect and manage the area. Soon after, imperial messengers were sent to Bai Jian to take custody of the horses and deliver them to Dingzhou to be entrusted to the populace to raise and feed.

### Awaiting Feeding <note>original: "待飼"</note>
The Book of Tang <note>original: "Tang Shu"</note>, in the Biography of Lu Zhi, records: Lu Zhi observed that soldiers from Henan, Jiangnan, and the Huai River region were mobilized year after year to the northwestern frontiers, an assignment termed "Autumn Defense." The soldiers were not well trained, and they suffered repeated defeats in battle. Military command was disunified, leaving no effective means to confront the enemy. He thereupon submitted a memorial detailing the harms, stating: "Counting the days until their return, they merely hold open their mouths like hungry fledglings awaiting feeding. If the army suffers even a single setback, they seize upon the danger and confusion, scattering eastward across the roads in collapse. In peacetime, state assets and granary stores are thoroughly exhausted to support idle and redundant troops; when crises arise, they abandon cities and strategic garrisons, shaking the stability of the frontier regions."

Essential Techniques for the Peasantry <note>original: "Qimin Yaoshu"</note> states: "Train and adjust tools and implements, striving to make them sharp and efficient; forage-feed the cattle and livestock, keeping them constantly fat and robust."

Prime Tortoise of the Record Bureau <note>original: "Cefu Yuangui"</note> records: In the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era <note>792 AD</note>, Pei Yanling submitted a memorial stating: "Stable horses in the winter months should remain at the mangers for forage feeding. Cao Tang, in his poem A Sick Horse, writes: "Though one morning sick, its heart to run a thousand miles still remains; how could it be willing to secretly forget the grace of forage feeding?"

Remaining Discourses of the Eastern Belvedere <note>original: "Dongguan Yulun"</note> records: Liu Yuanfu transcribed the inscription of the Qi Zhong Yi vessel into clerical script, stating: "Qi Zhong made this precious rectangular basket <note>original: "fu"</note>, choosing metal to cast, refine, and temper it in the furnace, turning it reddish, deep dark, and yellow, using it to hold various grain offerings and polished rice, using it to produce great harmonious sounds. ### As if Fed <note>original: "如飼"</note>
Biographies of Divine Transcendents <note>original: "Shenxian Zhuan"</note> records: Shen Jian once set out on a long journey, leaving one female servant, three male servants, one donkey, and ten sheep in the care of a host. He gave each a medicinal pill and told the host: "They will only take up house space; do not bother with food or drink." After Shen Jian departed, the host offered drink and food to the servants, but upon smelling the vapor of the food, the servants all retched and vomited, declining to eat. The host tried to feed grass to the donkey and sheep, but the donkey and sheep turned away and would not eat. After more than a hundred days, the servants' appearances were lustrous and glowing, looking healthier than when they ate normal food, and the donkey and sheep were all fat.

For thirty years, you accumulated the five grains to feed provisions to birds and insects. Calculated in this way, the cost is not less than the price of medicine."

This passage explains that if one makes <term>jing</term> <gloss>reverent attentiveness</gloss> primary, both internal and external become austere and calm, and the mind is naturally preserved.

If one makes <term>jing</term> <gloss>reverent attentiveness</gloss> primary, inner and outer become solemn and austere. One does not forget, nor does one artificially assist, and the mind is naturally preserved. But if one does not know how to make reverent attentiveness primary and merely wishes to hold fast and preserve the mind, one inevitably ends up using one mind to grasp another mind. When outside there is not yet a single disturbance, inside there are already divided threads and conflicting thoughts, completely overwhelmed by turbulent confusion. Even if one were truly able to seize and hold it fast, this alone would already be a major affliction. How much more so when one cannot truly seize and hold it fast!

The difference between Confucianism and Buddhism is demarcated precisely at this point. When people speak of "constantly seeing this mind brightly shining," that creates two separate controlling masters. In that case, does the shining light represent the true mind, or does the one who observes it represent the true mind?

Another passage says: "Now, when someone suddenly sees an infant about to fall into a well, because movement is triggered, their heart of commiseration becomes visible. ### <term>Kan</term> <gloss>The Abysmal Water Hexagram</gloss>

<term>Yichuan</term> <gloss>Cheng Yi</gloss> said: <term>Xi</term> <gloss>repeated</gloss> means practiced repetition. Although the other hexagrams are doubled, the character for repetition is not added to their names. Only <term>Kan</term> <gloss>The Abysmal Water</gloss> adds the word <term>xi</term> <gloss>repeated</gloss>, showing repeated peril, where within peril there is danger once again. Its meaning is vast indeed. 

In every case, when a yang line is on top, it is the image of stopping. When yang is in the middle, it is the image of falling into pit or snare. When yang is below, it is the image of moving. When a yin line is on top, it is the image of joy and pleasure. When yin is in the middle, it is the image of clinging and brightness. When yin is below, it is the image of gentle submission. Falling into the depths constitutes danger. 

<term>Xi</term> <gloss>repetition</gloss> means doubling. Just as in learning and practicing, or reviewing and practicing, both carry the meaning of repeating and doing again. <term>Kan</term> <gloss>The Abysmal</gloss> means danger and peril. What this hexagram speaks of is the way of dwelling amid peril and hardship.

The saying that "three for heaven and two for earth establish the reliance on numbers" <note>quoting the *I Ching*, Shuo Gua</note> means that by relying on the fundamental numbers of heaven and earth, the operational numbers of the *Changes* are established. Regarding the section on "attainment" <note>referring to Confucius's description of true inner moral breakthrough in Analects 12.20</note>, one must interpret it by closely adhering to the primary intent of this chapter. The line "straightforward by nature and loving righteousness" describes him as simple, solid, and free of ostentation. The two lines "examining words and observing expressions" describe him as restrained and not self-indulgent. What is noted as "acting in accord with what is right" differs from what is called elsewhere "adapting to the times to establish what is appropriate." A person of genuine hidden cultivation simply does what should be done according to his present station, never acting bizarrely or throwing aside his fundamental duty to perform some extraordinary feat to astonish the world. This is precisely where his hidden cultivation takes hold. "Examining and observing" does not mean prying into other people's joy or anger; it speaks entirely of his own self-reflection, self-questioning, caution, and reverence. The Sage deliberately introduced this line to lay the groundwork for "taking a lower place before others," without emphasizing self-examination alone. "Taking a lower place before others" means restraint, yielding, and avoiding an imposing, self-important posture; it is the opposite of being uninhibited and reckless, not simply the opposite of arrogance.

The section on "renown" stands in contrast to the above in every phrase; all of it consists of schemes hatched within the den of fame. These are precisely the scholars of a decadent age who engage in empty talk about heart-nature. The general thrust of the phrase "straightforward by nature" means that throughout life one is plain and honest, not engaging in superficial adornment, and in action aims solely to accord with what is right. Being straightforward by nature is in itself the foundation of loving righteousness; it does not mean tempering straightforwardness from the outside through tactful compromise. "Substance" is viewed in contrast to superficial decoration; "straightforwardness" is viewed in contrast to pretension and falsehood. A sincere heart has only a single path with no crooked detours; a false heart possesses a thousand paths and ten thousand tracks.

Another passage says: "When someone nowadays suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well, it is because of this arousal that their heart of commiseration becomes visible. From this we know that the former passage was surely recorded without full comprehension, or contains clerical errors. Master Luzhai happened to see only the former passage and did not consult the latter, hence this shortcoming. Because the Recorded Sayings were compiled by the diverse hands of many disciples, wherever doubtful points arise, one ought to cross-examine and compare various accounts in search of clarity, rather than hastily clinging to a single isolated statement as a definitive conclusion.

The Correct Meaning: Zheng Kangcheng says: "Entering first on the right" means entering the gate and turning right. "The shaman stops" refers to the rule that when the ruler travels, he must be accompanied by a shaman. The shaman is primarily tasked with warding off ominous and evil influences. Offering vegetable sacrifices <note>original: "釋菜"</note> serves to pay reverence to the gate deity. The necessity of paying reverence to the gate deity arises because, according to ritual, unless inquiring about an illness or condoling a bereavement, a ruler does not enter the homes of his various ministers. "The host outside the chamber facing south" means that the son of a grand master is of noble standing, so he is permitted to ascend the hall to witness the encoffining <note>the great encoffining ritual, <term>dalian</term></note>.

Kong Yingda says: This clarifies the rites for the great encoffining of a grand master. "The host" is the principal son. He goes out through the gate to welcome the ruler, but catching sight of the ruler's horses' heads, he does not wail and does not bow. He returns ahead of the ruler, enters the gate, and stands on the right facing north to await the ruler's arrival. He does not wail because he is overwhelmed by the presence of the ruler, not daring to give vent to his personal sorrow. "The shaman stops outside the gate" means that when a ruler attends the funeral of a minister, the shaman and the invocation priest carry peach-wood boughs and reed brooms <note>to exorcise noxious spirits</note> as far as the gate. Fearing that the host would find this distressing, and furthermore out of ritual respect for the host, he does not take the shaman inside to face the corpse and coffin. ### Six in the third place: Do not take a woman who sees a wealthy man and cannot maintain her person. There is no advantage. The Image says: Do not take a woman; her conduct is not compliant.

<term>Yichuan</term> <gloss>Cheng Yi</gloss> said: The third line, being yielding <term>yin</term>, resides in darkness and ignorance. It is neither central nor correct, representing a woman who acts rashly. Her proper resonant partner is above <note>line six</note>, but she cannot follow it from afar. Seeing nearby that nine in the second place is where the ignorant multitudes turn, flourishing at the height of its time, she abandons her proper resonant partner to pursue it. This is a woman seeing a wealthy man. When a woman follows a man, she should proceed according to proper ritual. Yet seeing that someone has much wealth, she delights in him and follows him, unable to maintain her own person. There is nowhere she can go that will bring advantage. When a woman acts like this, her conduct is perverse, corrupt, and non-compliant; she cannot be taken.

The line 'straightforward in substance and fond of righteousness' <note>original: "質直好義"</note> expresses his unadorned simplicity and lack of showiness. The two phrases 'observing others' words and examining their expressions' express his inward restraint and absence of unrestrained indulgence. The phrase 'what he does is fitting' in the commentary differs from 'adapting to circumstances according to time' found elsewhere. A scholar of genuine hidden cultivation merely does what ought to be done within his proper station; he never indulges in the bizarre or strange, discarding his fundamental role to perform shocking or sensational deeds. This is precisely where his hidden cultivation takes hold. 'Observing and examining' does not mean spying on the pleasures and angers of others; it refers entirely to his own self-reflection, self-questioning, caution, and reverent awe. The Sage specifically provided this line to lay the foundation for 'taking care to humble oneself beneath others,' with absolutely no emphasis on merely judging oneself. Humbling oneself beneath others denotes inward containment, restraint, and yield, refusing to adopt a grandiose, arrogant demeanor. It is the direct opposite of reckless abandon, not merely the opposite of pride. If one interprets it merely as courteous modesty, the original meaning is lost.

This section explains that taking reverence as primary allows inner and outer to become solemn and serene, so that the mind naturally preserves itself.

If one takes <term>jing</term> <gloss>reverence / seriousness of mind</gloss> as primary, then inner and outer are solemn and serene: without forgetting, without artificially assisting, and the mind is naturally preserved. But if one does not know how to take reverence as primary and merely desires to preserve the mind, one inevitably uses one mind to grasp and hold onto another mind. When outside there is not yet a single affair, inside there are already many tangled threads and chaotic impulses, producing an unbearable disturbance. Even supposing that one could truly grasp and hold onto it, this in itself would already be a great malady. How much more so when one cannot even truly grasp and hold it!

The difference between Confucianism and Buddhism also divides precisely here. If one says that one constantly sees this mind shining brilliantly, that means there are two masters. Does one not know whether the shining one is the true mind, or the seeing one is the true mind?

Examining what Lu-zhai stated, it was evidently rooted in this passage. Thinking carefully about it, there is ultimately an obstacle: since it says "at the initial moment of alarm and commiseration when the infant falls into a well," how can one also speak of it as "not yet having formed alarm and commiseration"?

Another passage says: "When people today suddenly see an infant about to fall into a well, because it stirs into manifestation, one sees their commiserating mind. Thus we know the former passage must have been imperfectly recorded by a student, or contains errant characters. Lu-zhai happened to see the former passage and did not consult the latter passage, hence falling into this oversight. <meta>continues from previous page</meta>As for "the ruler descending," having finished touching the corpse, he descends from the hall. "Causing the master of the house to ascend" means the ruler commands him to ascend. The master ascends by the western steps, proceeds from the foot of the corpse facing west, and leans over the corpse, taking care not to occupy the exact place where the ruler stood. The ruler also commands the mistress of the house to lean over it. In the "Rites for Mourning an Officer" <note>Shi sang li</note>, the son is not permitted to ascend; hence Zheng's commentary notes that the son of a great officer is honorable and therefore permitted to ascend to witness the encoffining.

Editorial remark: In the "Rites for Mourning an Officer," when the ruler presents vegetable offerings upon entering the gate, the commentary and subcommentary explain it as presenting vegetable offerings to honor the gate deity, which agrees exactly with the interpretation of vegetable offerings in this record. Kong's Subcommentary: Spreading the garments, arranging the positions, and the decorum of men and women are all entirely like those for a great officer.

<term>Master Kong Yingda</term> stated: This explains the encoffining ritual for an ordinary officer. Top Six: Wading across the river, submerged over the top of the head. Misfortune, yet no blame. The Image says: The misfortune of wading across the river cannot be blamed.

Master Yichuan <note>Cheng Yi, Song dynasty Neo-Confucian philosopher</note> said: Top Six occupies the ultimate extremity of excess by means of yin-yielding quality. This represents a petty person at the very peak of exceeding ordinary bounds. What is termed "great exceeding" in the case of a petty person does not mean they are capable of performing deeds that surpass others. It simply means exceeding ordinary bounds and transgressing principle, paying no heed to danger or ruin, and walking directly into peril and disaster. It is like crossing water to the point of being completely submerged over the top of the head. The misfortune is obvious. For petty persons to bring disaster upon themselves through rash agitation is only what they deserve. How could any external blame be placed upon it?

Master Yichuan said: <term>Xi</term> <gloss>repeated practice or duplication</gloss> refers to doubling. Although other hexagrams are doubled, the word is not added to their names. Only Kan has <term>Xi</term> added, which indicates repeated danger. Danger followed by further danger is of great significance. In all cases, yang above gives the image of stopping; in the middle, the image of falling into pitfall; below, the image of moving. Yin above gives the image of pleasing; in the middle, the image of clinging; below, the image of gentleness. Pitfall constitutes danger. <term>Xi</term> means repetition, just as in studying and reviewing, which carry the sense of repeating. Kan is danger; what the hexagram speaks of is the way to dwell in danger and difficulty. Kan is water; the number One begins in the center, being the earliest of all generated things. Therefore it constitutes water, and sinking into danger is the true substance of water.

Master Nanxuan <note>Zhang Shi, Song dynasty philosopher</note> said: Qian <note>Heaven</note> sings the lead and Kun <note>Earth</note> harmonizes. Qian is honorable and Kun is humble; this arises from natural order and cannot be disrupted.

Gen is mountain, Dui is marsh: the mountain is able solidly to bear the myriad things and make them grow, whereas the marsh cannot bestow its moistening effect unless it depends on existing things. Therefore, even with the yielding darkness of a woman, one should still accept what is good in her, and then one's clarity will be expanded. Furthermore, because all the other lines are yin, it speaks of a woman: if the second line can embrace and accept them, it can successfully assist in the affairs of its ruler, just as a son is able to manage his household. That a son is able to manage his household is due to the father's exclusive trust in him. The firm and yielding dispositions of the second and fifth lines connect with each other; therefore, the second line is able to carry out its way of firm centrality and accomplish the work of dispelling youthful ignorance.

In terms of the hexagram's talents, the second line is the teacher of the fifth. Six in the third place: Do not take this woman in marriage. She sees a man of bronze and does not maintain her person. Nothing is advantageous. The Image says: "Do not take this woman in marriage," for her conduct is not compliant.

Yichuan <note>Cheng Yi, the Northern Song Neo-Confucian master</note> said: The third line occupies youthful ignorance with yin yielding. It is neither central nor correct, representing a woman who moves rashly. Her proper resonance is at the top, yet she cannot follow it from afar. Seeing nearby that the nine in the second place is where the crowd of the ignorant turn, flourishing in its proper season, she abandons her proper resonance and follows him. This is what is meant by a woman seeing a man of bronze.
