The ritual states that the shaman halts outside the temple gate, while the invocator replaces him. Therefore, the invocator precedes the ruler in entering the gate and ascends by the eastern steps <term>zuojie</term> <gloss>the host's eastern staircase</gloss>. The ruler follows behind the invocator and ascends into the hall. He takes his position at the edge of the eastern partition wall <term>dongxu</term> <gloss>the eastern wall of the central hall</gloss>, to the east above the eastern steps. This is the place where the principal son and heir oversees the encoffining and shroud-dressing <term>lian</term> <gloss>the ritual encoffining and wrapping of the corpse</gloss>.

The host stands outside the chamber facing south because previously he stood to the right of the gate. When the ruler ascended, the host likewise ascended, standing to the north of the ruler and outside the eastern chamber, facing south, as both wish to view the encoffining and wrapping.

As for the moving of the corpse, previously the cords, shrouds, coverlets, and garments were laid out. Now that the ruler has arrived and all parties have taken their positions, they lift the corpse onto the laid-out garments.

When the host receives the announcement that the wrapping is completed, he descends the western steps to the bottom of the hall and stands facing north waiting for the ruler. Because the affection between ruler and subject is profound, they are about to part forever. Thus, when the wrapping is concluded, the ruler strokes the corpse's table with his hand to bid him farewell. Seeing the ruler stroke the corpse, the host bows and touches his forehead to the ground <term>kousang</term> <gloss>deep prostration with forehead touching the earth</gloss> at the foot of the hall to pay reverence to the ruler.

If one's clarity is devoted solely to trusting oneself, then one's virtue will not be broad. Therefore, even with the gentle obscurity of a woman, if she still accepts what is good, her clarity will become wide. Moreover, because the other lines are all <term>yin</term> <gloss>receptive and yielding energy</gloss>, the text refers to a wife. If the second line can contain and accept others, it can successfully assist its lord in his affairs, just as a capable son can manage his household. A son who can manage his household does so because his father places exclusive trust in him. The second and fifth lines join their feelings of the firm and the yielding. Therefore, the second line can carry out its path of firm balance and achieve the merit of dispelling ignorance <note>alluding to the Meng hexagram, "Enlightening Ignorance"</note>.

In terms of status and hierarchy, the fifth line represents the path of the father, while the second line represents the path of the son. In terms of the hexagram's talents, the second line serves as the teacher to the fifth line. The sages feared that the nine-in-the-second line might dwell arrogantly upon being the teacher, potentially losing the proper duty of a minister and son. Therefore, the sage cautioned him with the image of a son who can manage the household.

<summary>This passage comments on Hexagram Meng from the Book of Changes, analyzing the relationship between the second and fifth lines. It explains how a capable minister or teacher, represented as a filial son, must maintain humility and broad receptivity to serve his ruler properly.</summary>

Nanxuan <note>Zhang Shi, a prominent Neo-Confucian scholar and close colleague of Zhu Xi</note> wrote to Master Zhu discussing doubts concerning the Classics and masters, and raised this point; Master Zhu replied to him:

This passage means that if one takes <term>jing</term> <gloss>reverence, or focused mindfulness</gloss> as the primary foundation, then both inner thoughts and outer conduct become solemn and orderly, and the mind naturally preserves itself.

If one takes reverence as primary, inner and outer aspects become solemn, without forgetting and without artificial striving, and the mind naturally preserves itself. One who does not understand taking reverence as primary, but instead simply desires to preserve the mind, inevitably forces one mind to grasp and seize another mind. Before external affairs even arise, the inside is already split into multiple tangled threads, enduring unbearable turmoil. Even if one were truly able to seize hold of it, this in itself would already be a major fault; how much less can one actually seize and hold it?

The difference between Confucianism and Buddhism divides precisely on this point. For example, Buddhist sayings speak of "constantly seeing this mind shining brightly." That merely sets up two separate masters in command. Who can say whether the light that shines is the true mind, or the one that sees it is the true mind?

<summary>Zhu Xi responds to Zhang Shi's inquiries on self-cultivation, arguing that the mind is preserved naturally through inner and outer reverence rather than through forced self-monitoring, which creates an artificial split in the mind akin to Buddhist meditation errors.</summary>

If cloth and grain were used as currency, the damage caused would be immense. Cloth would be worn out and ruined in the hands of merchants and traders, and grain would be wasted and discarded in the course of measuring, cutting, and portioning. Viewed from this perspective, this proposal by Gong Yu <note>Gong Yu (貢禹, 124–44 BCE) was a Han dynasty official who advocated abolishing metallic coins in favor of silk cloth and grain</note> must certainly never be adopted. Even if in some remote region or subordinate town there are people who tear bolt-silk or discard grain to use them in place of coins, the authorities should still prohibit it. How much less should it ever be enacted as established law!

During the reign of Emperor Huan <note>Emperor Huan of the Later Han dynasty, reigned 146–168 CE</note>, a memorialist submitted a proposal stating: "Because our currency is light and valued commodities are meager, the people are driven into poverty. It would be fitting to recast coinage into larger denominations."

Liu Tao <note>Liu Tao (劉陶, died c. 185 CE), a Later Han scholar-official renowned for his memorials on state affairs</note> remarked: "The pressing worry of the present day does not lie in currency, but in the people's hunger. For the people could go a hundred years without currency, but they cannot endure a single day of starvation. Therefore, food is the matter of utmost urgency. Those debating this matter fail to understand agriculture and cultivation."

<summary>Qiu Jun critiques Gong Yu's historical proposal to replace metallic coinage with cloth and grain, arguing it causes severe economic waste, and cites Eastern Han official Liu Tao to emphasize that food security takes precedence over monetary reform.</summary>
<keywords>Qiu Jun, Gong Yu, Liu Tao, Emperor Huan of Han, currency reform, commodity money, coinage, food security, agriculture</keywords>
